The type of energy photons carry can be considered radiant energy. It is not kinetic because they have no mass. It can be argued that they have a relativistic mass, but certainly not a rest mass. A more proper equation of relativity is: E2 = (moc2)2 + (pc)2 Here we see energy, rest mass, and momentum related. p=mv is momentum for nonrelativistic particles. And yes, in order to travel at the speed of light, a particle cannot have (rest) mass.
A photon has no rest mass. They all possess energy, so any photon with a less-than-infinite wavelength has some mass. Not much, but not zero.

Photons are bosons (particles with integer spins), and as such are not limited by the Pauli exclusion principle, which is applicable to fermions (particles with half-integer spins). The exclusion principle states that two identical fermions cannot occupy the same quantum state at the same time. This gives an explanation for why electron orbitals in atoms appear the way they do (electrons are fermions). Since photons are not limited by this, technically there can be an infinite amount of photons in a given location, but photons always travel at the speed of light, so you can't collect and cram them anywhere.

But you could redirect them into a beam with a diamete of a single photon and they would be occupying the same space at the speed of light? In other words, they could occupy the same space, but you would be unable to keep them stationary.

Well, a photon doesn't have a diameter, it can be considered a point. However, if you were to somehow have a source that could generate a collimated beam of infinite photons (this is impossible, but for argument's sake let's say it could exist) then yes, the exclusion principle does not apply and you would be able to have an infinite number of photons travelling together, sharing the same quantum state at the same time.
